This function is called by dxfIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dxfInFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dxfInFields() returned.Call pFiler->atSubclassData(), passing in the string that was written out with group code 100 in dxfOutFields(). If this returns Adesk::kTrue, then continue. Otherwise immediately return an error status other than Acad::eOk (for example, Acad::eBadDxfSequence).Now read in the data. The DXF filer has only one readItem function which reads a single data item into a resbuf structure. The data read in must then be copied from the resbuf into whatever data member it belongs in. As of R13, it is possible to have order-dependent data. In custom classes you can have all order-independent, all order-dependent, or a mix of some order-independent and some order-dependent. For order-independent read in, use a loop that reads a single data item and then uses a switch statement or if-then-elseif chain to figure out what has been read in and place it into the appropriate data member. If an unexpected or unknown group code is read in, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong. Then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode). For order-dependent read in, use individual pFiler->readItem() calls to read each data item. Be sure to verify that each item read in is what it's supposed to be. If not, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong and then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence, or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode).

This function is called by dxfOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: 1. Call assertReadEnabled(). 2. Call the parent class's dxfOutFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned. 3. Use pFiler->writeItem(AcDb::kDxfSubclass, ), where is a string that is typically your class's name, but can be any string you wish up to 256 bytes long. This same string is used in dxfInFields(). 4. Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDxfFiler methods to write out the object's data items along with the appropriate group code values (see table below). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dxfOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus(). Here are the DXF group code ranges for object representation: From To Data Type 1 4 text 6 9 text 10 17 point or vector (3 reals) 38 59 real 60 79 16-bit integer 90 99 32-bit integer 100 100 subclass data marker 102 102 text 140 149 real 170 179 16-bit integer 210 219 3 reals 270 279 16-bit integer 280 289 8-bit integer 300 309 text 310 319 binary chunk 320 329 handle 330 339 soft pointer ID 340 349 hard pointer ID 350 359 soft owner ID 360 369 hard owner ID

Called from within close() before anything else is done. The default implementation is to return Acad::eOk. However, when overridden in custom classes, it provides a hook into the close operation. The [AcDbLine](https://cext-dan.github.io/CADPyRxDoc/PyDb.html#Line) class represents the line entity in AutoCAD. A line object is a 3D object that is specified by its start point, endpoint, and normal vector. In addition, the line object supports thickness along its normal vector direction (that is, height or 'extrusion').
This class is the symbol table for AcDbLinetypeTableRecords, which represent the linetypes within a drawing database.

This class is for iterating over the records in an AcDbLinetypeTable. The only substantial difference from the base class AcDbSymbolTableIterator is the use of AcDbLinetypeTableRecord-specific signatures for the member functions getRecord() and seek().

Possible return ErrorStatus codes are: Acad::eOk, Acad::ePermanentlyErased, Acad::eAtMaxReaders, Acad::eWasOpenForNotify, Acad::eWasNotifying, Acad::eWasOpenForUndo, Acad::eWasOpenForWrite, Acad::eWasOpenForRead

Objects of this class represent records in the AcDbLinetypeTable. Each of these records contains the information about a linetype in the drawing database. Within the LinetypeTableRecord, the dashes (line segments that make up characteristics of the linetype) are stored in a list with an index that is zero based. If the linetype is complex, then embedded shapes or text strings are stored in the list at the same index as the dash that preceded them in the linetype definition. So there will always be a dashLength for any valid index in the list, even if there is a shape or text string sharing the same index. When the linetype is elaborated, a shape's insertion point will coincide with the end of the dash that it shares an index with.

Returns Acad::eOk if successful. For more information on linetype definitions, see the 'Linetypes' section of the AutoCAD Customization Guide. The description string is used for DXF group code 3.

This function creates an iterator object that can be used to iterate through the contents of the LinetypeTable. pIterator is set to point to the newly created iterator object. This constructor initializes the line object to use start as the start point, and end as the endpoint. Both points must be in WCS coordinates.

This function creates one or more entities that, together, make up the result of offsetting the curve by the distance offsetDist in the plane with normal vector normal. For many curves, the result will be a single new curve, which may not be of the same class as the original curve. For example, offsetting an AcDbEllipse results in an AcDbSpline, since the result of offsetting an ellipse does not fit the equation of an ellipse. However, in some cases it might be necessary for the offset result to be several curves. To allow for this possibility, a dynamic array of void pointers is used to hold pointers to the resulting entity or entities. To use this array of pointers, the calling application must cast the pointer(s) to the appropriate object type(s). If only a specific entity type or set of types are to be handled, then using the cast method of the class(es) desired to see if each pointer can be safely cast to that object type will work. If the actual object type is desired, then each object's isA() method may be used to get a pointer to the object's AcRxClass object, which has a name() method to get the classname of the object. If the offsetDist value is negative this is usually interpreted as being an offset to make a smaller curve (that is, for an arc it would offset to a radius that is offsetDist less than the starting curve's radius). Or, if smaller has no meaning, then a negative offsetDist may be interpreted as an offset in the direction of smaller X,Y,Z WCS coordinates. However, this is not enforced, so custom entities can interpret the sign of the offsetDist value however they wish. The entities returned in the offsetCurves arrays are dynamically allocated, but have not been added to an AcDbDatabase yet. Returns Acad::eOk if offsetting is successfully completed. If the offset distance is invalid, or if normal is a zero length vector or the entity is linear and normal is not perpendicular with the entity, then Acad::eInvalidInput is returned. Other ErrorStatus return values are implementation dependent. The default implementation returns Acad::eNotImplemented.

This function is called by dwgIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgInFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to read in the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be read in, and in the same order, as those that are written out via dwgOutFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus reading in all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgInFields() implementation takes care of reading in the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dwgOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertReadEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgOutFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to write out the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be written out, and in the same order, as those that are read in via dwgInFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dxfIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dxfInFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dxfInFields() returned.Call pFiler->atSubclassData(), passing in the string that was written out with group code 100 in dxfOutFields(). If this returns Adesk::kTrue, then continue. Otherwise immediately return an error status other than Acad::eOk (for example, Acad::eBadDxfSequence).Now read in the data. The DXF filer has only one readItem function which reads a single data item into a resbuf structure. The data read in must then be copied from the resbuf into whatever data member it belongs in. As of R13, it is possible to have order-dependent data. In custom classes you can have all order-independent, all order-dependent, or a mix of some order-independent and some order-dependent. For order-independent read in, use a loop that reads a single data item and then uses a switch statement or if-then-elseif chain to figure out what has been read in and place it into the appropriate data member. If an unexpected or unknown group code is read in, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong. Then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode). For order-dependent read in, use individual pFiler->readItem() calls to read each data item. Be sure to verify that each item read in is what it's supposed to be. If not, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong and then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence, or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode).

This function is called by dxfOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: 1. Call assertReadEnabled(). 2. Call the parent class's dxfOutFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned. 3. Use pFiler->writeItem(AcDb::kDxfSubclass, ), where is a string that is typically your class's name, but can be any string you wish up to 256 bytes long. This same string is used in dxfInFields(). 4. Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDxfFiler methods to write out the object's data items along with the appropriate group code values (see table below). This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus(). This function loads the linetype specified by ltname from the file specified by fname and stores it in the database specified by pDb. Returns Acad::eBadLineTypeName if the file contains a malformed record, or a syntax error is encountered. Returns an appropriate Internet-specific Acad::ErrorStatus value if a URL is specified and the transfer is not successful.

Returns an appropriate Internet-specific Acad::ErrorStatus value if a URL is specified and the transfer is not successful.
This class represents a lofted surface entity. It provides methods to create and manipulate ASM surfaces.

Creates a lofted surface from the given curves using the specified options. The curves must be either all open or all closed. If the curves are all closed, then this function will accept a point entity as the first and/or last list entry. Each curve in the guideCurves list must intersect each of the cross-section curves, so the guide curves form a net-like structure with the cross-section curves. Both the cross-section curves and the guide curves will lie on the resulting surface. If any guide curves are passed in this list, then pPathCurve should be null. If pPathCurve is non-null, then the resulting surface will follow the shape of this curve as much as possible. This curve does not need to intersect the cross-section curves and does not even need to be near the cross sections. If this parameter is non-null, then guideCurves should be an empty list. Returns Acad::eOk upon successful creation. Returns Acad::eInvalidInput if the given data fails validation. Returns Acad::eFail if a surface cannot be created by ASM.

Utility class for setting options used by AcDbLoftedSurface::createLoftedSurface() . These options can be used to control the shape of the resulting surface. The default constructor for this class assigns default values to these options.
This is ==, a member of class AcDbLoftOptions.

Returns the value of the alignDirection option. This option can be used to orient each of the cross sections so that the normal vector of each cross section points towards the next cross section. The default value of this option is true. If the cross sections are not all oriented in the same direction, then this option should be used to avoid creating a twisted or self-intersecting surface or solid.

Checks whether cross section curves are valid for the lofting operation. This function is called by createLoftedSurface() and createLoftedSolid(), so it is not necessary for an application to call this function. Returns Acad::eOk if curves are valid, or Acad::eInvalidInput otherwise.

Checks whether guide curves are valid for lofting operation. This function is called by createLoftedSurface() and createLoftedSolid(), so it is not necessary for an application to call this function. Returns Acad::eOk if curves are valid, or Acad::eInvalidInput otherwise.

Checks whether cross section curves and guide/path curves are valid for the lofting operation. This function is called by createLoftedSurface() and createLoftedSolid(), so it is not necessary for an application to call this function. This function combines calls to check CrossSectionCurves(), checkGuideCurves(), and checkPathCurve() into a single function. Returns Acad::eOk if curves are valid, or Acad::eInvalidInput otherwise.
This function checks for valid combinations of options. Returns Acad::eOk if the current combination is valid.

Checks whether path curve is valid for lofting operation. This function is called by createLoftedSurface() and createLoftedSolid(), so it is not necessary for an application to call this function. Returns Acad::eOk if curves are valid, or Acad::eInvalidInput otherwise.

Returns the value of the closed option. If this option is set, then the resulting surface/solid will start and end at the first cross section. If all of the cross sections are closed, then this will result in a torus-like shape. If this option is not set, then the surface or solid will be open or capped with a planar surface at the first and last cross sections. The default value of this option is false. If this option is set, then there must be at least three cross sections.

Returns the end draft angle in radians. This is the surface take-off direction at the last cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which indicates that no draft angle is defined and the system will compute the optimum angle at the last cross section.

Returns the end draft magnitude. Controls the magnitude of the surface tangent vector at the last cross-section. The default value of this option is 0, which means that the system will compute the optimum magnitude.

Returns the start draft angle in radians. This is the surface take-off direction at the first cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which indicates that no draft angle is defined and the system will compute the optimum angle at the first cross section.

Returns the start draft magnitude. Controls the magnitude of the surface tangent vector at the first cross-section. The default value of this option is 0, which means that the system will compute the optimum magnitude.
Returns the plane normal option. See AcDbLoftOptions::NormalOption for a description of possible values. The default value of this option is kNoNormal.

Returns the value of the noTwist option. This option can be used to minimize the amount of twist in the resulting surface or solid when the cross-sections are all closed. The default value of this option is true. If this option is set then the start point of each closed cross-section is aligned with the other cross-sections to minimize twist.

Returns the value of the ruled option. If this option is set then a ruled surface will be created between each pair of cross sections rather than a single smooth surface. This will result in a much coarser object. The default value of this option is false.

Sets the value of the alignDirection option. This option can be used to orient each of the cross sections so that the normal vector of each cross section points towards the next cross section. The default value of this option is true. If the cross-sections are not all oriented in the same direction, then this option should be used to avoid creating a twisted or self-intersecting surface or solid.

Sets the closed option. If this option is set, then the resulting surface/solid will start and end at the first cross section. If all of the cross-sections are closed, then this will result in a torus-like shape. If this option is not set, then the surface or solid will be open or capped with a planar surface at the first and last cross sections. The default value of this option is false. If this option is set then there must be at least three cross sections.

Sets end draft angle. This is the surface take-off direction at the last cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which indicates that no draft angle is defined and the system will compute the optimum angle at the last cross section.

Sets the end draft magnitude. Controls the magnitude of the surface tangent vector at the last cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which means that the system will compute the optimum magnitude.

Sets start draft angle. This is the surface take-off direction at the first cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which indicates that no draft angle is defined and the system will compute the optimum angle at the first cross section.

Sets the start draft magnitude. Controls the magnitude of the surface tangent vector at the first cross section. The default value of this option is 0, which means that the system will compute the optimum magnitude.
Sets the plane normal option. See AcDbLoftOptions::NormalOption for a description of possible values. The default value of this option is kNoNormal.

Sets the value of the noTwist option. This option can be used to minimize the amount of twist in the resulting surface or solid when the cross sections are all closed. The default value of this option is true. If this option is set then the start point of each closed cross section is aligned with the other cross sections to minimize twist.
Set loft options from the current values of system variables.

Sets the ruled option. If this option is set then a ruled surface will be created between each pair of cross sections rather than a single smooth surface. This will result in a much coarser object. The default value of this option is false.

Sets the simplify option. If this option is set, then simple surface types (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, or torus) will be created whenever all of the cross sections lie on such a surface. Otherwise, a general surface type will be created. The default value of this option is true.
Sets the system variables from loft options.

Returns the value of the simplify option. If this option is set, then simple surface types (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, or torus) will be created whenever all of the cross sections lie on such a surface. Otherwise a general surface type will be created. The default value of this option is true.
Returns state of the virtual guide option.

This class is used to represent a profile that can be used as input to createLoftedSurface(). An object of this class can represent an entity such as a curve or a region, or it can represent an edge or a set of edges that form a connected chain. This class also maintains continuity data if the profile is for an edge or point and the profile is the first or last profile of the loft.
Constructor for a profile that is a point.
Returns the continuity for the profile: 0, 1, or 2, which corresponds to a continuity of G0, G1, or G2. By default, the continuity is 1 unless it has been explicitly set to another value.
This is copyFrom, a member of class AcDbLoftProfile.
Returns the magnitude of the takeoff vector if the continuity is 1 or 2. By default, this value is 0.5 unless it has been explicitly set to another value.
Sets the continuity for the profile.
Sets the magnitude of the takeoff vector for the profile if the continuity is 1 or 2.

This is the class that contains the information needed to track a long transaction. The AcLongTransactionManager class takes the responsibility for creating and appending AcDbLongTransaction objects to the database. It then returns the AcDbObjectId of the object. Destruction of this object is handled by the database (like other database resident objects).
Default constructor. Construction is handled by the AcLongTransactionManager class, and destruction is handled by the AcDbDatabase in which the object has been appended.

This function provides access to the cloning IdMap during AcLongTransactionReactor callbacks. The IdMap for CheckOut will not be the same as the IdMap used for CheckIn. Different cloning techniques will be used for each type of CheckOut/CheckIn for each Transaction Type. In all cases, the activeIdMap will be the IdMap used for the cloning. Just as in any deepClone operation, this IdMap also serves to identify the other deepClone notification callbacks. Returns the AcDbIdMapping* pointer which is currently being used for checkout/checkin or NULL, if not actively doing any cloning.

This function adds the object specified by the objectID, id, to the current work set. The object must be from the same space/BTR as the work set objects in the checked out database, that is the database in which the transaction resides. This function will accept objects from either the destination block, or the origin block. Objects from the origin block will not be cloned, but will be treated just like objects which followed a null object ID in the AcApLongTransactionManager::checkOut() list.
This function returns the objectID of the Block Table Record into which the objects are being be cloned.

This function returns true if a long transaction has been initiated by the REFEDIT command that includes only some of the entities from the source block that participate in the block's draw order. In this case, draw order information would be lost, so this check is used to disable the DRAWORDER command for the length of this REFEDIT session. This function returns false if it is not necessary to disable draw order manipulation.

Returns the name of the long transaction. For identification purposes, this is normally the name of the origin block. However, if the origin block is an Xref, it returns the name of the Xref Block in the host drawing. If the block is a Layout, it returns the name of the Layout.

This function creates an iterator for the work set. The default work set includes only the objects checked out from origin objects in the objList passed into checkOut(), and any objects from the checkout database which have been added later. If the incRemovedObjs parameter is true, the iterator will also include objects which have been removed from the work set, or have been erased. If the incSecondaryObjs is true, the iterator will include all objects which have been cloned into the checkout database. This means that objects that the primary objects depend upon, and have hard references to, will be included.
Returns the block from which the entities are checked out.

This will function determine the original objectID for the object provided by id. If the object is in the work set, it returns the original object from which the work set object was cloned. The function will return AcDbObjectId::kNull if the object is not found in the work set. If the object was added to the work set using addToWorkSet(), it returns the same AcDbObjectId passed in.

This function regens the work set defined in the long transaction, in the order defined by the ACAD_SORTENTS dictionary on the destination block used in the long transaction. This allows entities to be displayed in draw order during a REFEDIT session. If the SORTENTS kSortEntsRegen bit is off, or there is no ACAD_SORTENTS dictionary on the destination block, then the call has no effect.

This function removes an object from the work set. The result of this call is that the object becomes a permanent part of the checkout database, and if it originated from the origin database, its original object will not be updated during checkIn. Possible return values are: ENoActiveTransactions If the work set has not yet been created or checked out. eNullObjectId If the id is NULL. EKeyNotFound If the id is not found in the work set.

When an object has been placed in a work set, all of the objects that object owns are also added. If it is a lUnrelatedDb or kXrefDb type of long transaction, all referenced objects are also added. For the sake of performance, these referenced objects are not always removed by removeFromWorkSet(). So, this function completely cleans up any objects in a work set that are no longer referenced. It can be called after a number of removeFromWorkSet() calls, and is always called by the long transaction manager at checkIn time.

This function will return the type of transaction under way. Possible return values are: kSameDb If the entities have been checked out from a normal block within the same database. kXrefDb If the entities have been checked out from either Model Space, or an Xdep block in an Xref database. kUnrelatedDb If the entities have been checked out from Model Space or a block in a database which is either a temporary database within the same document, or a database from a different document.
Returns true if the object is in the work set. It returns false if the object is not in the work set, or if bIncErased is false and the object is in the work set, but has been erased.

Provides read-only access to the objects in the work set. During the construction of an AcDbLongTransWorkSetIterator object (by AcDbLongTransaction::newWorkSetIterator), it can be set to include only the active work set, or to also include objects which were added to the work set because they are referenced by objects in the work set (secondary objects), and/or objects which have been removed from the work set, either by AcDbLongTransaction::removeFromWorkSet(), or by being erased.
Indicates whether the current object has been erased. Returns true if the current object has been erased or false otherwise.

Indicates whether the current object is a primary object in the work set (for example it exists in the work set as a direct clone of an object in the origin set, or has been added). Returns true if the current object is a primary object in the work set. Returns false if the object is in the work set only because it is referenced by a primary object.
Indicates whether the current object has been removed from the work set. Returns true if the current object has been removed or false otherwise.
This function returns true if the iterator has been positioned past either end of the list of objects being iterated through, otherwise it returns false.
This function returns the AcDbObjectId of the object at which the iterator is currently positioned.
This function repositions the iterator to the first entity that it would normally return. This provides the ability to do multiple traversals of the modified list.
This function moves the iterator to the next object in the workset.

This method formats field code using the specified components. The field expression can be a simple field name like Date or Filename, or a complex expression like a diesel expression. The hyperlink sublocation should be same as the one used for the AcDbHyperlink object.

The AcDbMatchProperties class is an abstract base class for a series of protocol extension classes that add the ability to copy properties between entities. Derived classes for all the built-in entity types are provided as a part of the match.arx application. For custom classes that are not a part of AutoCAD, the custom class's application may derive its own class from the AcDbMatchProperties base class (and hook an object of the class into the run-time tree in the normal manner for protocol extension) in order to tie into the existing match properties interface that comes with AutoCAD (in match.arx).

This method is expected to copy any appropriate properties from pSrcEntity to pTrgEntity. flag is a set of bit flags indicating which properties to copy over. The enumerated type provides some predefined bits for the flag argument. The flag argument is an int so that you can make use of the unused bits for your own purposes. The predefined values are: enum Flags { kColorFlag= 0x1, kLayerFlag= 0x2, kLtypeFlag= 0x4, kThicknessFlag = 0x8, kLtscaleFlag = 0x10, kTextFlag = 0x20, kDimensionFlag = 0x40, kHatchFlag= 0x80, kLweightFlag = 0x100, kPlotstylenameFlag = 0x200, kSetAllFlagsOn = 0x3FF }; It is the caller's responsibility to be sure that pSrcEntity is open for read and pTrgEntity is open for write.

The AcDbMaterial class is used to define, store, and display material properties for shaded entities. An AcDbMaterial object consists of a variety of shading components, including diffuse, ambient, specular, reflection, opacity, bump, and refraction. Each component defines a different aspect of shading behavior for an entity. AcDbMaterial objects are stored in the ACAD_MATERIAL dictionary within the named object dictionary of an AcDbDatabase.
Gets the ambient component of the material.
Gets the bump component of the material.

Returns the channel flags for this material. The flags indicate which textures are in use by this material. Valid channel flags are: AcGiMaterialTraits::kNone, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseDiffuse, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseSpecular, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseReflection, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseOpacity, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseBump, and AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseRefraction. AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseAll contains bits for all the channel flags.
Obtains the color bleed scale value for the material.
Returns the pointer to the material description string. As the const qualifer indicates, do not attempt to deallocate the returned string.
Gets the diffuse component of the material.
Returns a pointer to the AcGiDrawable for the object. If the object doesn't have an associated AcGiDrawable object, this function returns NULL.

This function is called by dwgIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgInFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to read in the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be read in, and in the same order, as those that are written out via dwgOutFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus reading in all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgInFields() implementation takes care of reading in the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dwgOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertReadEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgOutFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to write out the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be written out, and in the same order, as those that are read in via dwgInFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dxfIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dxfInFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dxfInFields() returned.Call pFiler->atSubclassData(), passing in the string that was written out with group code 100 in dxfOutFields(). If this returns Adesk::kTrue, then continue. Otherwise immediately return an error status other than Acad::eOk (for example, Acad::eBadDxfSequence).Now read in the data. The DXF filer has only one readItem function which reads a single data item into a resbuf structure. The data read in must then be copied from the resbuf into whatever data member it belongs in. As of R13, it is possible to have order-dependent data. In custom classes you can have all order-independent, all order-dependent, or a mix of some order-independent and some order-dependent. For order-independent read in, use a loop that reads a single data item and then uses a switch statement or if-then-elseif chain to figure out what has been read in and place it into the appropriate data member. If an unexpected or unknown group code is read in, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong. Then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode). For order-dependent read in, use individual pFiler->readItem() calls to read each data item. Be sure to verify that each item read in is what it's supposed to be. If not, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong and then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence, or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode).

This function is called by dxfOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: 1. Call assertReadEnabled(). 2. Call the parent class's dxfOutFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned. 3. Use pFiler->writeItem(AcDb::kDxfSubclass, ), where is a string that is typically your class's name, but can be any string you wish up to 256 bytes long. This same string is used in dxfInFields(). 4. Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDxfFiler methods to write out the object's data items along with the appropriate group code values (see table below). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dxfOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus(). Here are the DXF group code ranges for object representation: From To Data Type 1 4 text 6 9 text 10 17 point or vector (3 reals) 38 59 real 60 79 16-bit integer 90 99 32-bit integer 100 100 subclass data marker 102 102 text 140 149 real 170 179 16-bit integer 210 219 3 reals 270 279 16-bit integer 280 289 8-bit integer 300 309 text 310 319 binary chunk 320 329 handle 330 339 soft pointer ID 340 349 hard pointer ID 350 359 soft owner ID 360 369 hard owner ID

Returns the illumination model set on this material. This model determines the type of shader used to render this material. The illumination model affects the color of light reflected from the material. The Blinn shader reflects the color of the light, whereas the Metal shader reflects a light color that is a combination of the color of the light and the material's diffuse color.
Obtains the indirect bump scale value for the material.

Returns an indication that the material is 'anonymous' in that it is intended for programmatic usage via API only, and should not be exposed through any user interface. Returns Adesk::kTrue if the material is anonymous in that it should be accessible only via API, otherwise Adesk::kFalse if it is exposed via user interface. The default is Adesk::kFalse.
This is isRenamable, a member of class AcDbMaterial.
Obtains the luminance value of the material.
Obtains the luminance mode of the material.
Returns the mode of this material.
Returns the pointer to the material name string. As the const qualifer indicates, do not attempt to deallocate the returned string.

Stores the material map for the normal map channel of the material, the method used to compute the normal map, and the channel strength. Returns an Acad::ErrorStatus representing the error return if the AcDbMaterial advanced parameters are unable to be read from the extension dictionary, otherwise, Acad::eOk.
Gets the opacity component of the material.
Obtains the reflectance scale value for the material.
Gets the reflection component of the material.
Returns the refelectivity of the material. A higher value indicates a highly reflective material.
Gets the refraction component of the material.
Returns the self-illumination property of the material.
Sets the ambient color component of the material. The ambient color affects the overall color of the entity and is most noticeable where the entity receives no direct illumination.

Sets the material 'anonymous' flag, to indicate that this material is for programmatic usage only via API, and is not to be exposed via user interface. Returns Acad::eOk if successful; otherwise, returns an AutoCAD error status.
Sets the bump component of the material. The bump component gives a raised or depressed appearance to the surface of the entity.

Sets the channels in use by this material. This allows multiple channels to be added to a material and each channel to be enabled or disabled individually. Valid channel flags are: AcGiMaterialTraits::kNone, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseDiffuse, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseSpecular, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseReflection, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseOpacity, AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseBump, and AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseRefraction. AcGiMaterialTraits::kUseAll contains bits for all the channel flags.
Sets the Advanced Material parameter for Color Bleed Scale. Returns Acad::eOk if a valid color bleed scale value is passed in.
Sets the diffuse component of the material. The diffuse component is most noticeable where the entity is directly illuminated.
Sets the final gathering mode. The default value is AcGiMrFinalGatheringMode::krFinalGatherAuto.

Sets the illumination model used by the renderer to render this material. The illumination model affects the color of light reflected from the material. The Blinn shader reflects the color of the light, whereas the Metal shader reflects a light color that is a combination of the color of the light and the material's diffuse color.
Sets the Advanced Material parameter for Indirect Bump Scale. Returns Acad::eOk if a valid indirect bump scale value is passed in.
Sets the mode of this material.

This function sets the material name by copying the input name. It can be used to rename a material. If the name is already in use by another material, does not change the existing name and returns an error. The characters in the description can be Unicode, multibyte representations or multibyte characters On success returns Acad::eOk.

Sets the material map for the normal map channel of the material, the method used to compute the normal map, and the channel strength. Returns Acad::ErrorStatus representing an error condition if the normal map could not be stored in the extension dictionary of the material, otherwise, Acad::eOk.
Sets the opacity component of the material. The opacity component makes it possible to see through the entity.
Sets the Advanced Material parameter for Reflectance Scale. Returns Acad::eOk if a valid reflectance scale value is passed in.
Sets the reflection component of the material. The reflection component is responsible for a mirror-like finish on an entity.
Sets the reflectivity of the material. Use this in conjunction with setReflection(), to set the degree of reflectivity.
Sets the refraction component of the material. The refraction component lets an entity be seen through in such a way that light appears to be bent.
Sets the self-illumination property on the material.
Sets the shininess model for this material. Returns Acad::eOk if the shininess model was set successfully.
Sets the specular component of the material. The specular component is noticeable where the entity is highlighted and dependent on the viewpoint.
Sets the translucence value of the material. Returns Acad::eOk on success.
Sets the Advanced Material parameter for Transmittance Scale. Returns Acad::eOk if a valid transmittance scale value is passed in.
Sets the TwoSided flag. Determines whether the material applies to both sides of each face.
Returns the shininess value of the material.
Gets the specular component of the material.
Returns the translucence value of the material.
Obtains the transmittance scale value for the material.
Returns true if the material is two sided.
This class is a container for all properties relating to the Mental Ray renderer.

Function usage: Copies the contents of other into the messaged object, whenever feasible. Function implementation in derived classes: If implemented, this function needs to be able to read the data in the object pointed to by other and copy any or all data as appropriate into this object. There is no requirement that the object pointed to by other and this object be of the same class, but that is the generally assumed condition. Default implementation: Because this function must be overridden to have any meaning, a fatal error will be caused when calling the default implementation.

Returns the coordinate system to use for the diagnostic grid, including the distance between grid lines (size).
Returns the mode used for rendering diagnostic images.
Returns the type of photon information to visualize with the photon diagnostic mode.

Returns Boolean indicating whether to export an MI file after rendering.
Returns the full path and file name to use for an exported MI file.
Returns the export to mi mode.
Returns the number of final gather rays to be used for each final gather point.
Returns the minimum and maximum radii of the area used to sample final gather points to compute indirect illumination.
Returns the flags indicating whether the user-defined final gathering sampling radii are used, and what units they are defined in.
Returns a Boolean value indicating whether final gathering is applied.
Returns the average number of GI photons to shoot for each light.
Returns the maximum number of photons near a render sample point to use for computing global illumination.
The radius of the area used to sample photons for global illumination.
Returns a Boolean value indicating whether the user-defined photon sampling radius is used.
Returns a Boolean value indicating whether global illumination (using photon mapping) is computed.
Returns the physical scale factor to use with lights that are not physically based.
Returns the maximum amount of memory (in MB) that the renderer will allocate for rendering.
Returns the maximum trace depth (recursion level) for photons.
Returns the maximum trace depth (recursion level) for rays.
Returns a Boolean value indicating whether ray-tracing is performed.
Returns the minimum and maximum numbers of samples to take when shading a pixel during rendering.

Returns the threshold above which further samples will be taken, per color channel. When performing sampling, the renderer will compare a sample to its surrounding samples, and take further samples if the difference is greater than the threshold value.
Returns the filtering parameters for combining multiple samples into a single pixel color.
Sets the type of BSP information to visualize with the BSP diagnostic mode. The default value is krDepth.

Sets the coordinate system to use for the diagnostic grid including the distance between grid lines (size). The grid size must be greater than zero. The default mode is krObject and the size is 10.0. Returns Acad::eOk if the specified grid size is valid.
Sets the mode for rendering diagnostic images. The default value is krOff.
Sets the type of photon information to visualize with the photon diagnostic mode. The default value is krDensity.
Sets the energy multiplier value. This is the equivalent illuminance for calculating indirect illumination.
Sets whether to export an MI file after rendering. The default value is false. If set to true, the file name specified with setExportMIFileName() is used to save the MI file.
Sets the full path and file name to use for an exported MI file. The default value is blank. Returns Acad::eOk if the file name is valid.
Set the export to mi mode. The default value is AcGiMrExportMIMode::krExportMIOff.
Sets the flags indicating whether the user-defined final gathering sampling radii are used, and what units they are defined in.

Sets the number of final gather rays to be used for each final gather point. The indicated number of rays are shot into the scene for each final gather point to compute indirect illumination. This value must must be greater than zero. The default value is 1000. Returns Acad::eOk if the final gather ray count count value is valid.
Sets the minimum and maximum radii of the area used to sample final gather points to compute indirect illumination. Returns Acad::eOk if the radius values are valid.
Final gathering allows for indirect illumination effects such as color-bleeding, and can be combined with photon mapping to enhance the effect of global illumination. The default value is false.

Sets the maximum number of photons near a render sample point to use for computing global illumination. Sets the radius of the area used to sample photons for global illumination. If the photon sampling radius is not used, a default radius based on the model extents is used. The default value is false.
Global illumination provides indirect illumination effects such as photon-mapping. The default value is false.

Sets a physical scale factor to use with lights that are not physically based. Sets the maximum amount of memory (in MB) that the renderer will allocate for rendering. After the memory limit is reached, the renderer makes performance tradeoffs to stay under the memory limit. The AcDbMline class represents the AutoCAD MLINE entity. This multi-line entity allows the user to create a complex line with multiple parallel line parts, each with its own linetype. The space between these parallel lines can be filled if desired.

AcDbMlineStyle class objects are used to store the information about the number, linetypes, and offsets of multi-line line patterns to be used by AcDbMline entities. An mline style consists of a series of elements, each of which is a line at a given offset from an axis (there may or may not be an element on the axis). AcDbMlineStyle objects are stored in the ACAD_MLINESTYLE dictionary within the Named Object Dictionary of AcDbDatabase.
No initialization done in this constructor.

Adds a new element to the AcDbMlineStyle. The elements index in the element list is returned in index. The offset, color, and lineTypeId arguments are all used to specify the desired properties of the new element. If checkIfReferenced is true and the mline style object is referenced, then the add operation will be aborted and Acad::eObjectIsReferenced will be returned. This indicates that it is not safe to change this mline style object. Returns Acad::eOk if successful.

Function usage: Copies the contents of other into the messaged object, whenever feasible. Function implementation in derived classes: If implemented, this function needs to be able to read the data in the object pointed to by other and copy any or all data as appropriate into this object. There is no requirement that the object pointed to by other and this object be of the same class, but that is the generally assumed condition. Default implementation: Because this function must be overridden to have any meaning, a fatal error will be caused when calling the default implementation.

Returns a pointer to the description string for the MlineStyle object. The description string is not used by AutoCAD--it is provided as a place to store some descriptive text about the MlineStyle. The description string shows up in the 'Description' edit box of the MLineStyle dialog in AutoCAD. The description string can be up to MSTYLE_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH in length (see dbmstyle.h for actual value). The pointer points to the actual internal string, not a copy, so do not attempt to delete the string.

This function is called by dwgIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgInFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to read in the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be read in, and in the same order, as those that are written out via dwgOutFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus reading in all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgInFields() implementation takes care of reading in the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dwgOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertReadEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgOutFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to write out the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be written out, and in the same order, as those that are read in via dwgInFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dxfIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dxfInFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dxfInFields() returned.Call pFiler->atSubclassData(), passing in the string that was written out with group code 100 in dxfOutFields(). If this returns Adesk::kTrue, then continue. Otherwise immediately return an error status other than Acad::eOk (for example, Acad::eBadDxfSequence).Now read in the data. The DXF filer has only one readItem function which reads a single data item into a resbuf structure. The data read in must then be copied from the resbuf into whatever data member it belongs in. As of R13, it is possible to have order-dependent data. In custom classes you can have all order-independent, all order-dependent, or a mix of some order-independent and some order-dependent. For order-independent read in, use a loop that reads a single data item and then uses a switch statement or if-then-elseif chain to figure out what has been read in and place it into the appropriate data member. If an unexpected or unknown group code is read in, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong. Then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode). For order-dependent read in, use individual pFiler->readItem() calls to read each data item. Be sure to verify that each item read in is what it's supposed to be. If not, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong and then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence, or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode).

This function is called by dxfOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: 1. Call assertReadEnabled(). 2. Call the parent class's dxfOutFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned. 3. Use pFiler->writeItem(AcDb::kDxfSubclass, ), where is a string that is typically your class's name, but can be any string you wish up to 256 bytes long. This same string is used in dxfInFields(). 4. Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDxfFiler methods to write out the object's data items along with the appropriate group code values (see table below). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dxfOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus(). Projects newVertex along the MLine object's normal vector onto the plane defined by the normal vector and the first vertex of the MLine object. The result of this projection is appended to the end of the MLine object's vertex list. This generates a new MLine object segment between the previously 'last' vertex and the newly added vertex. After segments are appended, AcDbMline::setClosedMline() must be called to close the MLine object. Returns Acad::eOk if the new vertex is successfully appended. If the MLine object doesn't have a valid MlineStyle reference set, then Acad::eInvalidStyle is returned. If the MLine object doesn't have a valid normal set, then Acad::eInvalidNormal is returned.

Used to determine if the MLine object is currently closed (that is, there is a closing segment that joins the last and first vertices). Returns true if the MLine object is currently closed. Otherwise it returns false.

This function attempts to find which element of the MLine object contains the point pt. If an element is not found that directly contains the point and the MLine object is not closed, then the ends of the MLine object are 'virtually' extended to see if pt lies in the path of any element. If successful, the index number of the element (see AcDbMlineStyle for an explanation of elements) that contains pt is returned. If not successful, then -1 is returned.

In this function, givenPoint is projected along the normal vector onto the plane containing the MLine object. Then the resulting projected point is used to find the point on the MLine object that is closest. pointOnCurve is filled in with the closest point found. If extend == true, then the MLine object will be 'virtually' extended to find the closest point. If excludeCaps == true, then any endcaps on the MLine object will be ignored. Returns Acad::eOk if function call is successful.

Returns the current scale value in use by the MLine object. The scale value controls the overall width of the MLine object. This scale doesn't affect linetype scale. The scale factor is based on the width established in the MlineStyle definition. A scale factor of 2 produces an MLine object twice as wide as the style definition. A negative scale factor flips the order of the offset lines--the smallest on top, when the MLine object is drawn from left to right. A negative scale value also alters the scale by the absolute value. A scale factor of 0 collapses the MLine object into a single line. For information on the MlineStyle definition, see AcDbMlineStyle and the MLSTYLE command in the AutoCAD User's Guide.

Since the normal vector data member is used to define the projection plane for any new vertices, if this function is called after the MLine object contains more than one vertex, the result will a non-planar MLine object, which can lead to very unpredictable behavior. This function is called by dwgIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgInFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to read in the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be read in, and in the same order, as those that are written out via dwgOutFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus reading in all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgInFields() implementation takes care of reading in the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dwgOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertReadEnabled().Call the parent class's dwgOutFields() passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise, immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned.Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDwgFiler methods to write out the object's data items. It is essential that the same number of data items be written out, and in the same order, as those that are read in via dwgInFields(). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dwgOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus().

This function is called by dxfIn(). Its purpose is to allow the object to read in its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: Call assertWriteEnabled().Call the parent class's dxfInFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dxfInFields() returned.Call pFiler->atSubclassData(), passing in the string that was written out with group code 100 in dxfOutFields(). If this returns Adesk::kTrue, then continue. Otherwise immediately return an error status other than Acad::eOk (for example, Acad::eBadDxfSequence).Now read in the data. The DXF filer has only one readItem function which reads a single data item into a resbuf structure. The data read in must then be copied from the resbuf into whatever data member it belongs in. As of R13, it is possible to have order-dependent data. In custom classes you can have all order-independent, all order-dependent, or a mix of some order-independent and some order-dependent. For order-independent read in, use a loop that reads a single data item and then uses a switch statement or if-then-elseif chain to figure out what has been read in and place it into the appropriate data member. If an unexpected or unknown group code is read in, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong. Then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode). For order-dependent read in, use individual pFiler->readItem() calls to read each data item. Be sure to verify that each item read in is what it's supposed to be. If not, use pFiler->pushBackitem() to rewind the file pointer back to the item that was wrong and then return immediately with an appropriate error status (such as Acad::eBadDxfSequence, or Acad::eInvalidDxfCode).

This function is called by dxfOut(). Its purpose is to allow the object to write out its data. There is a fixed set of steps that should be followed when implementing your own version of this function: 1. Call assertReadEnabled(). 2. Call the parent class's dxfOutFields(), passing it pFiler. If this returns Acad::eOk, then continue; otherwise immediately return whatever the parent class's dwgInFields() returned. 3. Use pFiler->writeItem(AcDb::kDxfSubclass, ), where is a string that is typically your class's name, but can be any string you wish up to 256 bytes long. This same string is used in dxfInFields(). 4. Use pFiler to call the appropriate AcDbDxfFiler methods to write out the object's data items along with the appropriate group code values (see table below). Following these steps results in all base classes having their implementations of this function called as well, thus writing out all the object's data in class hierarchical order. The actual AcDbObject::dxfOutFields() implementation takes care of writing out the object's handle as well as its persistent reactor, extension dictionary, and xdata information. This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. In your own custom class implementations of this function, it's easiest to just return pFiler->filerStatus(). Handles one or more closed polygons as a unit. Contains an AcDbHatch member for rendering and other tasks, via AcDbMpolygon::hatch( ).

Returns Acad::eOk if the boundary has been added. If excludeCrossing is true and the boundary is rejected, Acad::eAmbiguousInput is returned. For a boundary to be considered crossing, it must cross by at least tol amount. Touching is not considered crossing. The tolerance is scaled according to the boundary edges being operated on. Crossing boundaries may cause unpredictable inner and outer boundary type assignments during MPolygon creation or rebalancing, as well as unpredictable MPolygon hatch rendering.

Appends a new boundary loop to the AcDbMPolygon entity. Vertices contains a set of AcGePoint2d objects. Bulges contains a set of double values. Vertices and bulges must correspond one to one. However, an empty bulges set can be passed into the function if the loop contains all line segments only. If excludeCrossing is true and the boundary is rejected, Acad::eAmbiguousInput is returned. For a boundary to be considered crossing, it must cross by at least tol amount. Touching is not considered crossing. The tolerance is scaled according to the boundary edges being operated on. Crossing boundaries may cause unpredictable inner and outer boundary type assignments during MPolygon creation or rebalancing, as well as unpredictable MPolygon hatch rendering. Returns Acad::eOk when successful. Otherwise, returns Acad::eInvalidInput or Acad::eAmbiguousInput.

This function is called by AutoCAD when the AUDIT command is executed. The AcDbAuditInfo object pointed to by pAuditInfo contains member functions that are used to determine what to do and also to report the results of the audit operation on the object. When overriding this function for a custom class, if conditions are correct, this function should return Acad::eOk. If there's an internal problem, the object should call the pAuditInfo argument's fixErrors() member. If Adesk::kTrue is returned, and the object can successfully repair itself, it should do so, and return Acad::eFixedAllErrors. If the object cannot successfully repair itself, it should return Acad::eUnrecoverableErrors. If Adesk::kFalse is returned from fixErrors(), and the object has internal errors, it should leave them be, and return Acad::eLeftErrorsUnfixed. Here is a sample audit function from the ARXLABSLAB09JBLOB.CPP file: Acad::ErrorStatusJblob::audit(AcDbAuditInfo* pAuditInfo){ if (mrblob <= 0.0) { pAuditInfo->errorsFound(1); if (pAuditInfo->fixErrors() == Adesk::kTrue) { char buff[50]; sprintf(buff, '%f', mrblob); pAuditInfo->printError('JBLOB', buff, '> 0.0', '0.2 * line length'); // no way to know what the radius really should be // so make it about 0.2 of the line length as a // reasonable guess so that it'll at least be visible // on screen. // mrblob = 0.2 * mpblob.distanceTo(mp); pAuditInfo->errorsFixed(1); return Acad::eFixedAllErrors; } else return Acad::eLeftErrorsUnfixed; } else return Acad::eOk;}

Removes degenerate boundaries from the internal AcDbMPolygon hatch entity or inserts boundaries that are no longer degenerate back into the internal AcDbMPolygon hatch entity. Calls balanceDisplay() after loop boundary edit operations to ensure that the AcDbMPolygon displays correctly. A degenerate boundary is a boundary that crosses itself or another boundary in the AcDbMPolygon, an inner boundary not inside an outer boundary, or an outer boundary inside an outer boundary. Degenerate boundaries are removed from the internal AcDbMPolygon hatch entity so that they do not fill. They are still drawn, but they are drawn as simple polylines without fill.

Does an analysis of the AcDbMPolygon containment tree and marks nodes (boundary loops) as outer or inner. If a node is on an odd tree level (level 1, 3, 5, ...), it is marked as outer; otherwise it is marked as inner. Inner boundary vertices are set to clockwise order. Outer boundary vertices are set to counter-clockwise order. Calls balanceDisplay() to remove degenerate loops from the internal AcDbHatch entity, and then calls evaluateHatch() to compute hatch pattern lines. Returns Acad::eOk if all boundaries have been marked as outer or inner. The UI command MPOLYGON calls balanceTree() to automatically set inner and outer boundaries during AcDbMPolygon creation after all boundaries have been added. The UI command MPEDIT REBALANCE calls balanceTree() to rebalance the AcDbMPolygon boundaries.
This function creates loops for the polygon. Returns Acad::eOk if successful.
Create loops from boundaries. Returns Acad::eOk if successful.

This member function is used to control behavior for custom objects and entities when saving to previous formats. Custom objects can decompose themselves into other objects and can add additional xdata to the objects created. The default implementation of this function sets replaceObj to NULL and replaceid to AcDbObjectId::kNull so that no decomposition is done. If this is overridden, the custom object can create any number of new objects. It has to return one of them as a replacement object and the original is subsequently deleted by ObjectARX. The function can either return an AcDbObjectId in replaceId or it can return an AcDbObject* in replaceObj. If the object pointer is returned, ObjectARX adds the entity to the database. Only one of replaceObj or replaceId should be returned. In both cases ObjectARX transfers the objectId from the original to the replacement so that inter-object references are maintained. If decomposeForSave() is overridden in an custom object, the exchangeXData argument should be set by the new implementation of decomposeForSave to indicate to ObjectARX whether or not to transfer xdata from the original to the replacement. If the custom object's implementation of decomposeForSave() does not add any new xdata, and decomposeForSave() returns with exchangeXData set to Adesk::kTrue, then ObjectARX transfers all existing xdata from the original object to the replacement. If exchangeXData is set to Adesk::kFalse, then the existing xdata is left with the original object. exchangeXData is set to Adesk::kTrue in the internal implementation so the default behavior will be to transfer xdata. Overriding this method will allow the application to handle the xdata transfer itself or let ObjectARX handle it. If the custom object's implementation of decomposeForSave() adds any xdata to the replacement, then it must also deal with transferring all xdata from the original to the replacement if that xdata is to be preserved. It should set exchangeXData to Adesk::kFalse to indicate that ObjectARX is not to transfer any xdata. It is not possible for the implementation of decomposeForSave() to add new xdata to the replacement object and then return with exchangeXData == Adesk::kTrue in order to have ObjectARX transfer the existing xdata from the original to the replacement. If this is done, then the result is the loss of all the xdata added inside decomposeForSave(). This function should return Acad::eOk if successful. Any other return status terminates the operation.

The getMPolygonTree() function allocates and returns a tree of AcDbMPolygon nodes that mirror the internal containment tree of the AcDbMPolygon. This tree can be used to determine node nesting and which node is inside which other node. This function sets the pointer to point to the root node of the tree that it produces. The root node has AcDbMPolygonNode member variable mLoopIndex equal to -1. If getMPolygonTree() is successful, it returns Acad::eOk. The caller must call deleteMPolygonTree() to delete the AcDbMPolygonNode objects that getMPolygonTree() allocated; otherwise there will be memory leaks. Example of use: AcDbMPolygonNode * rootNode;pMPolygon->getMPolygonTree(rootNode); Do analysis of node nesting while converting boundaries to Oracle formatpMPolygon->deleteMPolygonTree(rootNode);

Returns the AcDbMPolygon offset vector. Whenever an AcDbMPolygon gets created or rebalanced through a call to AcDbMPolygon::balanceTree() or when the AcDbMPolygon::transfromBy() function is called, a new offset vector gets created. The offset vector is the center point of the extents of the AcDbMPolygon. After the offset vector is computed, the true vertices of all AcDbMPolygon boundaries get subtracted by the offset vector. This calculation is done to improve AcDbMPolygon computation precision with very large numbers. AcDbMPolygon boundaries get serialized in the offset space. Operations such as evaluateHatch(), transformBy(), getOsnapPoints(), intersectWith(), grip editing, crossing calculations, inside and outside tests, and area and perimeter calculations are all done in the AcDbMPolygon offset space.

Inserts a new boundary loop to the AcDbMPolygon entity. The loopIndex argument specifies the index at which the loop will be inserted into the AcDbMPolygon boundary loop list. The vertices argument contains a set of AcGePoint2d objects. The bulges argument contains a set of double values. Vertices and bulges must correspond one to one. However, an empty bulges set can be passed into the function if the loop contains only line segments. If excludeCrossing is true and the boundary is rejected, Acad::eAmbiguousInput is returned. For a boundary to be considered crossing, it must cross by at least tol amount. Touching is not considered crossing. The tolerance is scaled according to the boundary edges being operated on. Crossing boundaries may cause unpredictable inner and outer boundary type assignments during MPolygon creation or rebalancing, as well as unpredictable MPolygon hatch rendering. Function usage This function is used by AutoCAD to generate the graphic primitives whenever a DWG save is occurring that requires proxy graphics to be saved for the entity. Overriding this function allows control of the graphics that will be stored. It is possible for an ObjectARX application to call this function, but it will need to provide a fully functional AcGiWorldDraw object and the AcGiWorldGeometry and AcGiSubEntityTraits objects for which it provides references. The only way to do this is to derive custom classes from these three AcGi classes. The acgisamp.cpp sample program supplied with the ObjectARX SDK demonstrates how to do this. Function implementation in derived classes The AcGiWorldDraw object pointed at by pMode, as well as the AcGiWorldGeometry and AcGiSubEntityTraits objects available from the AcGiWorldDraw object, are all provided to allow this function to generate whatever graphics primitives are desired to represent the entity when it is displayed as a proxy. The ObjectARX Developer's Guide explains how to use these classes. In the contexts that this function is called, there is no need to deal with GS marker assignments. However, all the visible properties such as colors, layer, linetypes, visibilities, etc. are relevant. The st argument provides the context for the call of this function. The graphics primitives generated by this function will be stored with the entity in the drawing file so that if the drawing is ever loaded up with the entity's controlling application not loaded (that is, the entity becomes a proxy), the entity can still be displayed. Default implementation By default, this method calls the entity's worldDraw() method using the mode pointer.

This function runs through the MText object's text string breaking it up into fragments, calling the fragment elaboration function func for each fragment. If the default of NULL is used for the ctxt argument, the current AcGiWorldDraw object is used. The fragment elaboration function's prototype is: int (*AcDbMTextEnum)(AcDbMTextFragment *frag, void *param) The elaboration function is called once for each fragment. frag points to an AcDbMTextFragment structure that's passed into the elaboration function. frag provides all the information about the text fragment for which the elaboration function is being called. param contains the value (which is just a void* address) of the param argument passed into the explodeFragments() member function. param can point to anything desired--it is only passed on to the elaboration function func. param provides a means to pass application-specific data into the elaboration function. The elaboration function should return 1 to continue the elaboration operation, or 0 to terminate the operation. In the context of this function, a fragment is a piece of text that lies on the same 'word-wrapped' line and has a specific set of characteristics (that is, font, color, height, width, etc.). So, each word-wrap newline and each change in text characteristics starts a new fragment.
